judged_by: Matched by a Claude Opus 5.5 agent on 2026-11-22; not yet checked by the labeler.

question.note: Phrased as what the paper argues rather than as a question, but its subject is the spillover of the 'convicted criminal' ad onto perceptions of people with records (Q1).
The recommendation to elevate justice-involved voices instead of stigmatizing attacks is the central claim C2, not the question.
States the counter-narrative's mitigating effect; its subject is Q2. Could instead be read as a misplaced half of C1.

flags.text: 'Exposure to a stigmatizing label of Trump' attributes the effect to the label; the stimulus was the mugshot with the label, and the paper says the two cannot be disentangled (p.17). The quotes say 'advertisement with the ... label'.

central_claim.note: Gives the harm to perceptions and the counter-narrative's mitigation; omits that the ad improved feelings of representation, although the first quote says so.

evidence.note: Survey experiment with Democrats (E1 without pre-registration; Prolific and dates are in entry 4), the total N of 2,439 (E2 without arms; the arms are in the next entry), and the two outcome families (part of E4, given in full in entry 3).
Names the three arms, without the counts.
Counter-narrative half of E3 (assemblymember Jovan Jackson, named in the paper p.3). The ad stimulus is not described.
Prolific and the July 12-13, 2025 dates (the rest of E1; 2,500 recruited is the paper's pre-exclusion figure), plus the manipulation check on emotional reactions (E7).
Balance across arms (p.9) is accurate to the paper but not a gold answer.

flags.text: 'Exposure to a stigmatizing label of convicted criminal' attributes the effect to the label; the stimulus was the mugshot with the label, and the paper says the two cannot be disentangled (p.17). The quote says 'advertisement with the ... label'.

'The negative effects of stigmatizing language' attributes the ad's effect to the language; the paper's quote speaks of 'the negative effects of the advertisement', and image and label cannot be separated (p.17).

key_findings.note: Keeps the offset relation to the ad's effect, so no F-x2 flag.

flags.text: Says the counter-narrative increased perceived public-service motives of officials. The paper finds it reduced them relative to the ad alone (H1F, beta = -0.098, p.11, not robust to Bonferroni). The quote is a hypothesis. The value-of-representation half is accurate (H1C, p.11).

key_findings.note: No credit because half the entry is reversed.

flags.text: Says the ad reduced perceived public-service motives and the counter-narrative weakened this. The paper finds the ad increased belief that officials serve the public (beta = 0.130, p.11) and the counter-narrative reduced it (beta = -0.098). The quote is hypothesis H1D, about quality of representation.

'The counter-narrative significantly increases positive perceptions' drops that the counter-narrative came before the ad and is compared with the ad alone; there was no counter-narrative-only arm (p.16). The quote keeps the qualification.

key_findings.note: F2 is also credited in entry 1; a scorer may count it once.

scope_and_limits.note: Gives durability only (behavior is in entry 2).

The paper says replication 'in other contexts and in less-transparent designs is unclear' (p.17); the note recasts this as demographic or geographic contexts and names no consequence of the Democrats-only sample, so it does not reach L10. No credit, no flag (as in the first harnessed run).
Gives the gap to behavior; durability is in entry 0.

theoretical_positioning.note: Does not state the applies-and-extends stance (T4).

flags.text: Says the paper disputes a claim that stigmatizing language in political ads has no negative impact on perceptions. No one in the paper makes that claim; the quote is about negative campaign ads being used less by poll leaders and not aiding election success (I2), which the claim does not state.
